questions.question: Which statement best contrasts mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) as distortion metrics for scalar quantization?
questions.choice_A: MAE and MSE behave similarly, with identical sensitivity to outliers.
questions.choice_B: MSE penalizes large errors more heavily than MAE, making it more sensitive to outliers.
questions.choice_C: MAE penalizes large errors more heavily than MSE because it does not square errors.
questions.choice_D: MSE is always preferable to MAE for any source distribution and application.

questions.question: Which qualitative description best matches the rate–distortion behavior for scalar quantization under MSE?
questions.choice_A: Distortion decreases as bits increase, with diminishing returns; the curve is decreasing and convex in rate.
questions.choice_B: Distortion increases with more bits because decision regions become too small.
questions.choice_C: Distortion remains constant once more than 2 bits are used.
questions.choice_D: Distortion decreases linearly with the number of bits with no diminishing returns.

questions.question: Which summary correctly describes the Lloyd–Max algorithm for scalar quantization with known source pdf?
questions.choice_A: Randomly generate codepoints and keep the set with lowest empirical error on a held-out set.
questions.choice_B: Use equal-width bins and set reconstruction levels at bin edges.
questions.choice_C: Iteratively update decision boundaries to midpoints between neighboring reconstruction levels and update reconstruction levels to conditional means within each cell.
questions.choice_D: Sort samples and pick every $K$-th sample as the reconstruction levels.

questions.question: What are the first-order optimality (stationarity) conditions for an MSE-optimal scalar quantizer with a known continuous pdf?
questions.choice_A: Decision boundaries at codepoint means; codepoints at decision boundary midpoints.
questions.choice_B: Decision boundaries equally spaced; codepoints equally likely.
questions.choice_C: Codepoints at decision boundary medians; boundaries at codepoint medians.
questions.choice_D: Nearest-neighbor condition for decision boundaries and centroid condition for reconstruction levels.

questions.question: How do quantile (equal-mass) quantizers compare to MSE-optimal quantizers for a unimodal, smooth pdf?
questions.choice_A: MSE-optimal quantizers allocate more levels to high-density regions than equal-mass quantizers.
questions.choice_B: Equal-mass quantizers always minimize MSE by construction.
questions.choice_C: They are identical when the pdf is symmetric and unimodal.
questions.choice_D: Equal-mass quantizers place more levels in low-density regions than MSE-optimal ones.

questions.question: For a zero-mean Gaussian source and an MSE-optimal scalar quantizer with an odd number of levels, which property is expected?
questions.choice_A: Uniformly spaced reconstruction levels over the real line.
questions.choice_B: Reconstruction levels concentrated in the tails rather than near zero.
questions.choice_C: A symmetric codebook about zero with more densely packed levels near zero.
questions.choice_D: A single level at zero and decision boundaries at infinity.

questions.question: In the high-rate regime for scalar quantization under MSE, how does doubling the number of codepoints typically affect distortion?
questions.choice_A: Distortion remains approximately unchanged.
questions.choice_B: Distortion decreases by approximately a factor of 4 (i.e., $D \propto 2^{-2R}$).
questions.choice_C: Distortion decreases by approximately a factor of 2 (i.e., $D \propto 2^{-R}$).
questions.choice_D: Distortion increases because of overfitting to the source distribution.

questions.question: For a symmetric source and a symmetric scalar quantizer, what is the expected mean of the quantization error under MSE?
questions.choice_A: Strictly positive because positive errors dominate.
questions.choice_B: Strictly negative because negative errors dominate.
questions.choice_C: Undefined because the error distribution is heavy-tailed.
questions.choice_D: Approximately zero, due to symmetry of the source and quantizer.

questions.question: When might MAE be a more appropriate distortion metric than MSE for designing a scalar quantizer?
questions.choice_A: When the source is Gaussian and outliers are extremely rare.
questions.choice_B: When entropy coding is not available.
questions.choice_C: When robustness to outliers is desired, such as for Laplacian or heavy-tailed sources.
questions.choice_D: When equal-probability bins are required by the application.

questions.question: Which statement about the Lloyd–Max algorithm is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: It can converge to different local optima depending on initialization; multiple restarts are often beneficial.
questions.choice_B: It always finds the unique global optimum regardless of initialization.
questions.choice_C: It requires the source to be uniform to converge.
questions.choice_D: It is equivalent to picking quantiles of the empirical distribution.

questions.question: How does entropy coding interact with scalar quantization rate?
questions.choice_A: Entropy coding cannot reduce the average rate below $\log_2 K$ bits per sample.
questions.choice_B: Entropy coding can reduce the average rate toward the entropy of the quantizer index distribution, which can be less than $\log_2 K$.
questions.choice_C: Entropy coding increases distortion but reduces rate.
questions.choice_D: Entropy coding eliminates the need for quantization entirely.

questions.question: When is an equal-mass (quantile) quantizer particularly suitable?
questions.choice_A: When the objective is to minimize MSE under a known smooth pdf.
questions.choice_B: When preserving low-probability tail fidelity is the main objective.
questions.choice_C: When the source is uniform and the MSE-optimal quantizer is nonuniform.
questions.choice_D: When equal usage of indices, rank preservation, or monotonic transformations are important (e.g., robust downstream statistics).

questions.question: Under high-rate theory for MSE-optimal scalar quantization with source pdf $f(x)$, how should the cell width $\Delta(x)$ scale with density?
questions.choice_A: $\Delta(x) \propto f(x)^{-1/3}$, i.e., narrower cells where the pdf is larger.
questions.choice_B: $\Delta(x) \propto f(x)$, i.e., wider cells where the pdf is larger.
questions.choice_C: $\Delta(x)$ should be constant regardless of $f(x)$.
questions.choice_D: $\Delta(x) \propto f(x)^{-1}$, giving extremely narrow cells in the tails.

questions.question: For a Laplacian source under a bitrate constraint, why are dead-zone (wider) cells around zero commonly used in practice?
questions.choice_A: They minimize MAE but always increase MSE.
questions.choice_B: They are required for convergence of Lloyd–Max.
questions.choice_C: They increase the probability of the zero index, enabling better entropy coding efficiency while maintaining good MSE for sparse-like signals.
questions.choice_D: They equalize the probability of all indices.

questions.question: Which procedure provides a sound empirical estimate of the expected MSE distortion of a designed quantizer?
questions.choice_A: Evaluate distortion on the same finite training set used to design the quantizer, with no resampling.
questions.choice_B: Generate a large i.i.d. test set from the source (or a faithful model) and compute the sample mean of squared errors.
questions.choice_C: Report the minimal cell width as the distortion.
questions.choice_D: Count the number of codepoints used and divide by the number of samples.

questions.question: How does Lloyd–Max for a known pdf differ conceptually from k-means on a finite sample set?
questions.choice_A: Lloyd–Max uses gradient descent while k-means does not.
questions.choice_B: They are identical in all respects.
questions.choice_C: k-means updates boundaries using medians, whereas Lloyd–Max uses means.
questions.choice_D: Lloyd–Max computes conditional expectations and boundary midpoints with respect to the pdf, while k-means computes empirical averages over samples.

questions.question: Which distinction between granular and overload distortion is correct for scalar quantization?
questions.choice_A: Granular distortion arises only for unbounded sources; overload only for bounded sources.
questions.choice_B: Overload distortion refers to error within the interior cells; granular refers to clipping at the extremes.
questions.choice_C: Granular distortion is due to quantization within support (finite step-size effects), while overload distortion arises when samples fall outside the quantizer’s outermost decision regions (clipping).
questions.choice_D: Both distortions vanish at low rates.

questions.question: How should one think about choosing the number of codepoints $K$ under an average rate budget when entropy coding is allowed?
questions.choice_A: It can be beneficial to choose $K > 2^R$ if the index distribution is highly skewed, because the average rate approaches the entropy of the indices, which can be below $\log_2 K$.
questions.choice_B: One must always choose $K = 2^R$; any other choice is suboptimal.
questions.choice_C: Choosing $K < 2^R$ always reduces distortion.
questions.choice_D: Entropy coding forces all indices to be equally probable, so $K$ does not matter.

questions.question: For 1-bit scalar quantization of a zero-mean symmetric source under MSE, what is the optimal decision threshold?
questions.choice_A: At the mean plus one standard deviation.
questions.choice_B: At zero, because symmetry implies equal probability of positive and negative values.
questions.choice_C: At the median of the absolute value.
questions.choice_D: At any value; threshold choice does not affect MSE.

questions.question: Which is a practical and correct convergence criterion or property for the Lloyd–Max iterations?
questions.choice_A: Stop when all decision boundaries are equally spaced.
questions.choice_B: Stop when the average index entropy stops changing.
questions.choice_C: Stop after a fixed number of iterations because distortion oscillates arbitrarily.
questions.choice_D: The algorithm monotonically decreases (or leaves unchanged) the MSE each iteration; stop when the reduction in distortion or change in codebook/boundaries falls below a tolerance.
